passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of varying doses of the novel cognitive enhancer, NeuroBoost, on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design was employed. A total of 120 healthy adult volunteers were assigned to one of four groups: Placebo (n=30), Low Dose (5 mg, n=30), Medium Dose (10 mg, n=30), and High Dose (20 mg, n=30). After a single administration, participants completed a computerized choice reaction time task, and the mean response time (in seconds) and standard deviation were recorded. The results are summarized in Table 1 below. The data indicate a dose-dependent improvement, with the High Dose group exhibiting the fastest average reaction time and the lowest variability. These findings suggest that NeuroBoost enhances cognitive processing speed in a dose-responsive manner, consistent with pharmacodynamic principles. Further investigations are warranted to assess long-term effects and optimal dosing strategies.
stem: Which treatment group had the lowest average response time?
explanation: The table shows the High Dose group with an average response time of 0.54 s, the lowest among all groups.
trap: Treating the smallest SD (0.02 s, High Dose) as the fastest reaction time; SD measures spread, whereas the mean gives the speed.

trap: Some students mistakenly identify the lowest dose group as the control.

stem: Which variable, if it differed systematically among the four dose groups, could confound the apparent dose-response relationship for reaction time?

options.A: Mean age of participants in each group
options.B: The unit of time (seconds) used to report reaction time
options.C: The total sample size of 120 volunteers
options.D: The name of the compound being tested

explanation: Correct: A. Reaction time slows with age, so if older participants clustered in one group, group differences could reflect age rather than dose. Why the others are wrong: B) The unit is just a reporting convention applied identically to all groups and cannot alter results. C) The total sample size is a fixed number shared by the study and does not vary between groups in a way that biases outcomes. D) The name of a compound is a label and has no effect on measured reaction time.
trap: Picking a study feature that merely describes the experiment instead of a participant factor that independently affects reaction time.

stem: Which of the following best links the study's findings to the broader theory of dose-response relationships?

options.A: The results support a graded dose-response with diminishing returns per mg at higher doses
options.B: The results support a threshold effect
options.C: The results support a U-shaped curve
options.D: The results support a plateau at high doses

explanation: RT falls at every dose (0.68 to 0.54 s), but the gain per mg shrinks (about 0.012, 0.010 and 0.007 s/mg), so the relationship is graded and sublinear rather than strictly linear.
trap: Calling the curve strictly linear or a plateau: RT still improves at the highest dose, but not proportionally to dose.
